title: Three Ingenious Ways to Repurpose Your Old Kindle: Spotify Remote, Smart Display, or Literary Clock
summary: Amazon Kindles are excellent at displaying ebooks, but their E-Ink screens are capable of much more. If you've upgraded to a newer model or simply have an old one collecting dust, consider these three clever repurposing projects. They range from simple to complex, but all come with online instructions. First, you can turn your Kindle into a Spotify remote. This doesn't involve installing the Spotify app or storing music; instead, it leverages Spotify Connect. By entering your Spotify credentials and ensuring your Kindle is on the same Wi-Fi network as your playback device, you can control music, podcasts, or audiobooks directly from the e-reader. You can skip tracks, pause, and resume playback. It's a neat way to manage your listening without pulling out your phone. Second, with more effort, you can transform your Kindle into a smart display. Developer Matt Healy has documented the process, which involves setting up a custom website and possibly crafting a frame. The display can pull in real-time data from various services: weather forecasts, calendar events, to-do lists, and even delivery statuses. This project is ideal for learning about hardware hacking, coding, and API integrations. By the end, you'll have a personalized, always-on information dashboard. The information you display is limited only by the third-party services you connect to. Third, for book lovers, you can create a literary clock. This hack repurposes the Kindle into a timepiece that shows a different quote from a book for each minute of the day—all 1,440 of them. The quotes mention specific times, and the clock doesn't reveal the book or author unless you tap the screen, turning it into a literary quiz. All necessary images and scripts are pre-made, so you mainly need to follow setup instructions. You can build a stand or frame, but it's optional. These projects demonstrate that old Kindles are far from obsolete. With some tinkering, they can become functional, stylish additions to your home.
why_it_matters: Repurposing old electronics reduces e-waste, one of the fastest-growing environmental problems, and teaches valuable skills in coding and problem-solving. It shows that creative reuse can extend a device's life and make technology more personal and useful.

background_read: Amazon's Kindle (first released in 2007) revolutionized reading by using low-power E-Ink screens that mimic paper, leading to a decline in physical book sales.

E-Ink technology was originally developed at MIT's Media Lab in the 1990s and uses tiny microcapsules of charged particles to display text without a backlight, making it gentle on the eyes and energy-efficient.
As newer, faster models have come out, many older Kindles end up unused, but a vibrant DIY community has embraced these devices for creative repurposing, often sharing step-by-step guides online.

The projects mentioned tap into Internet of Things concepts, where everyday objects are connected to the internet to perform new functions—like a clock that pulls literary quotes from a pre-loaded database.
Spotify Connect, used in the remote project, is a protocol that lets any device on the same network control playback, similar to how many smart speakers work.

perspectives.description: These hacks give a second life to devices that would otherwise gather dust, offering custom, low-energy tools that save money and reduce electronic waste.
However, such projects may require technical know-how that not everyone has, and using an old device might lack security updates, potentially exposing users to risks if connected to the internet.
The phenomenon of 'device repurposing' reflects a growing maker culture that blends consumer tech with open-source software, challenging the idea that gadgets become useless after a few years.

As manufacturers are pressured to support longer product lifespans, these DIY solutions could influence future designs that prioritize modularity and hackability, making repurposing easier for everyone.
